<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js"
    integrity="sha256-FgpCb/KJQlLNfOu91ta32o/NMZxltwRo8QtmkMRdAu8=" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Contributing to Meshery CLI End-to-End Tests</h1>
          
          <p>Meshery CLI is the command line interface for Meshery. Meshery CLI, otherwise known as <code>mesheryctl</code>, is a client of Meshery Server&rsquo;s <a href="/v0.9/extensibility/api/">REST API</a>. It provides a way to interact with Meshery and perform various operations such as installing, configuring, and managing cloud native infrastructure.</p>
<p>This document is intended to help you contribute to the end-to-end tests for <code>mesheryctl</code>, the Meshery CLI. It is designed to be a guide for developers who are new to the project and want to contribute to the testing of <code>mesheryctl</code>.</p>
<p>The end-to-end tests for <code>mesheryctl</code> are designed to ensure that the CLI is working as expected and that it is compatible with the various cloud native infrastructure and public cloud services that Meshery supports. These tests are run automatically on every pull request to ensure that any changes made to the code do not break the existing functionality of the CLI.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Meshery CLI Reference Documents</div>
<ul><li><a href="/project/contributing/contributing-cli">Contributing to Meshery CLI</a></li><li><a href="https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1q63sIGAuCnIeDs8PeM-0BAkNj8BBgPUXhLbe1Y-318o/edit#gid=0">Meshery Command Tracker</a>: Status of mesheryctl command implementation and platform compatibility.</li>
    <li><a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xRlFpElRmybJ3WacgPKXgCSiQ2poJl3iCCV1dAalf0k/edit#">Meshery CLI Commands and Documentation</a>: Detailed documentation of the `mesheryctl` commands.</li>
	<li><a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/labels/component%2Fmesheryctl">mesheryctl open issues and pull requests</a>: Matching the "component/mesheryctl" label.</li></ul></div>
<h2 id="familiarizing-with-meshery-cli-end-to-end-testing">
	Familiarizing with Meshery CLI End-to-End Testing
</h2>
<p>End-to-end testing of <code>mesheryctl</code> uses the <a href="https://github.com/bats-core/bats-core">Bash Automated Testing System</a> (BATS) framework to define and execute CLI tests. Each test case is designed to mimic the experience that a Meshery CLI user might have while interacting with <code>mesheryctl</code> in their terminal of choice. In this sense, <code>mesheryctl</code> tests run end-to-end with each pull request submitted containing changes to either the <code>/mesheryctl</code> or the <code>/server</code> directories in the <code>meshery/meshery</code> repository, ensuring that changes included in those pull requests do not break the existing CLI functionality.</p>
<h3 id="prerequisites">
	Prerequisites
</h3>
<p>Before diving into <code>mesheryctl</code>&rsquo;s testing environment, certain prerequisites must be met to ensure a smooth testing experience. These prerequisites include:</p>
<ul>
<li>A working installation of Meshery CLI and Meshery Server.
<ul>
<li>A verified account in your chosen provider which integrate with Meshery.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>A working installation of the BATS testing framework.
<ul>
<li><code>bash</code> as shell terminal.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>[Optional] A working installation of a Kubernetes cluster (Minikube, Kind, etc.) for testing Kubernetes-related functionality.</li>
<li><code>jq</code> and <code>yq</code>, tools for processing JSON and YAML inputs, respectively.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="setup-bats-core">
	Setup Bats Core
</h3>
<p>For Bats Core, always try to use a BATS-native OS whenever possible. This is because BATS Core does not support Windows. If you are using Windows, you can use WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) to run BATS Core. See the official <a href="https://bats-core.readthedocs.io/en/stable/installation.html">BATS installation documentation</a> for more information on how to install BATS Core on your system. Here are quick start steps.</p>
<h4 id="macos-homebrew">
	MacOS (homebrew)
</h4>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">brew install bats-core
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="any-os-npm">
	Any OS (npm)
</h4>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">npm install -g bats
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="windows-from-source-via-bash">
	Windows (from source via bash)
</h4>
<p>Check out a copy of the Bats repository and install it to $HOME. This will place the bats executable in $HOME/bin, which will need to be added in $PATH.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">git clone https://github.com/bats-core/bats-core.git
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="nb">cd</span> bats-core
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">./install.sh <span class="nv">$HOME</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Some tests could use bats libraires as helpers to create the tests suite.</p>
<h4 id="setup-dependencies">
	Setup Dependencies
</h4>
<p>There are needed dependencies to test whether the server is up and running. Resolve them by navigating to <code>meshery/mesheryctl</code> directory and then executing:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">  make e2e-libs
</span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="starting-meshery-server">
	Starting Meshery Server
</h3>
<p>There are a few ways to set up the Meshery server, but for end-to-end testing, we aim to get as close to a production environment as possible. We know developers might need to make some tweaks for Server. Rebuilding the whole project can take time, and we don’t support hot reload because it’s more for development than for end-to-end testing.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">make server
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>Be aware that some test cases require the availability of a Kubernetes cluster and one or more  Meshery Adapters. In those cases, please refer to the <a href="/v0.9/installation/">installation guides</a>) (like that of <a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/minikube/">installing Meshery on Minikube</a>).</p>
<h3 id="authentication">
	Authentication
</h3>
<p>To run the tests successfully, you need be logged in to your Meshery account. This is required to access the Meshery Server and perform operations on it. Whether using the local or a remote provider, you will need to generate a token from your user account to use while writing and executing tests.</p>
<p><strong>Remote Provider Example</strong></p>
<p>If you are using Meshery Cloud as your remote provider, you can <a href="https://cloud.meshery.io/security/tokens">generate and download an API token</a> from your user account for use while writing and executing tests.</p>
<h3 id="verify-your-api-token">
	Verify your API Token
</h3>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">mesheryctl system check
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>If you see this error message - <code>Error: !! Authentication token not found. Please supply a valid user token. Login with mesheryctl system login</code>, you will need to authenticate using the command:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">mesheryctl system login
</span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="writing-end-to-end-test-cases">
	Writing End-to-End Test Cases
</h2>
<p>Once all prerequisites have been met, you are setup to run, add, update new test cases.To keep the development of tests consistents and maintainable, we have put some guidance on implementation process which are describe above.</p>
<h3 id="folder-structure">
	Folder structure
</h3>
<p>The tests will be available in<a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/tree/master/mesheryctl/tests/e2e"><code>mesheryctl/tests/e2e</code></a> folder with the following structure which is done to follow the code base structure of <code>mesheryctl</code>.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-shell" data-lang="shell"><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── aaa-&lt;command&gt;
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── bbb-&lt;command&gt;
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── ...
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── yyy-&lt;command&gt;
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── zzz-&lt;command&gt;
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── helpers
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── README.md
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── run_tests.bash
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── setup_suite.bash
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">└── teardown_suite.bash
</span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="test-case-naming-convention">
	Test Case Naming Convention
</h3>
<p>Bats will run the tests sequentially so we use a prefix code alphanumeric to be able to order tests as required  when necessary. The prefix code is used to order the tests in a way that makes sense for the command under test. The prefix code is used to group the tests by command and subcommand. The prefix code is also used to order the tests within the command and subcommand. For example, you need to import a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Meshery Model</a> before being able to view the details of that model</p>
<p><strong>Test Folder</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>prefix</strong>: 3 digits alphanumeric code</li>
<li><strong>name</strong>: command under test</li>
</ul>
<p>Example: <code>011-design</code></p>
<p><strong>Test File</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>prefix</strong>: 2 digits numeric code</li>
<li><strong>name</strong>: subcommand under test</li>
<li><strong>extension</strong>: bats</li>
</ul>
<p>Example: <code>05-list.bats</code></p>
<p>For consistency, we will keep the prefix <em>00-</em> for the command under test in the folder and subcommands will start at <em>01-</em>. Here an example with <code>mesheryctl model</code> command:</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">002-model/
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">├── 00-model.bats
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">└── 01-model-list.bats
</span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="run-end-to-end-locally">
	Run End-to-End (locally)
</h2>
<p>Make sure you are in <code>meshery/mesheryctl</code> directory</p>
<p><strong>Run all tests</strong></p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># run tests building mesheryctl binary</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">make e2e
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># run tests without buiding mesheryctl binary</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">make e2e-no-build
</span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Run a specific commmand tests suite</strong></p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">make e2e-no-build <span class="nv">BATS_FOLDER_PATTERN</span><span class="o">=</span>&lt;<span class="nb">test</span> folder name&gt;
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Example to run mesheryctl model subcommand tests</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">make e2e-no-build <span class="nv">BATS_FOLDER_PATTERN</span><span class="o">=</span>002-model
</span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Run a specific test file</strong></p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">make e2e-no-build <span class="nv">BATS_FOLDER_PATTERN</span><span class="o">=</span>&lt;<span class="nb">test</span> folder name&gt; <span class="nv">BATS_FILE_PATTERN</span><span class="o">=</span>&lt;<span class="nb">test</span> <span class="nb">command</span> name&gt;
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="c1"># Example to run mesheryctl model genereate tests</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">make e2e-no-build <span class="nv">BATS_FOLDER_PATTERN</span><span class="o">=</span>002-model <span class="nv">BATS_FILE_PATTERN</span><span class="o">=</span>06-model-generate
</span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>More on running tests locally</strong></p>
<p>Breaking down the execution of <code>make e2e</code>, two commands are executed before subsequent commands are run;</p>
<ul>
<li><code>make</code>: which builds the binary and</li>
<li><code>e2e-libs</code>: which gets needed dependencies for running the tests.</li>
</ul>
<p>These steps can become redundant if you&rsquo;re not running the end-to-end tests for the first time.</p>
<p>It is important to point out that there are other ways to run end-to-end tests locally.
To use these, ensure you are in the <code>meshery/mesheryctl/tests/e2e</code> directory.</p>
<p><strong>Run tests with already built binary</strong></p>
<p>This excludes the need to build the binary everytime there is an attempt to run all the tests.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">  bash run_tests_local.sh
</span></span></code></pre></div><p>NB: This works if there is an existing <code>mesheryctl</code> binary. If there isn&rsquo;t, the binary will be built.</p>
<p><strong>Enforce rebuilding the  binary</strong></p>
<p>This involves parsing a flag for the binary to be built whether it exists or not. This comes in handy when you have local changes and possibly will like to test.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">  bash run_tests_local.sh -b
</span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="find-tests-here">
	Find Tests here
</h3>
<p>Refer to <a href="https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/13Ir4gfaKoAX9r8qYjAFFl_U9ntke4X5ndREY1T7bnVs/edit?usp=sharing">Meshery Test Plan</a> for test scenarios.</p>
<p>To filter and view only CLI-related test cases using the Sheet Views feature:</p>
<ol>
<li>In the top menu bar, click Data → Change view</li>
<li>Choose the pre-defined view labeled &ldquo;CLI&rdquo;</li>
</ol>
<p><img class="content-image" src="/project/contributing/images/meshery-test-plan-v0.8.0-ui.png" alt="Meshery Test Plan Screenshot"  /></p>
<h2 id="developement">
	Developement
</h2>
<p><strong>End-to-End Tests:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Purpose:</strong> Validate the complete flow of an application, from the user interface (in this case, the <code>mesheryctl</code> CLI) down to the underlying systems (Meshery server, Kubernetes, etc.).</li>
<li><strong>Scope:</strong> Test multiple components working together to achieve a specific user scenario.</li>
<li><strong>Speed:</strong> Generally slower to execute compared to unit and integration tests as they involve setting up and interacting with a real or near-real environment.</li>
<li><strong>Cost:</strong> Can be more expensive to set up and maintain due to the complexity of the environment.</li>
<li><strong>Frequency:</strong> Typically run less frequently than unit and integration tests, often as part of continuous integration pipelines or release processes.</li>
</ul>
<p>For <code>mesheryctl</code>, E2E tests will focus on verifying that CLI commands perform their intended actions against a running Meshery instance <strong>in context of how users experience the CLI</strong>, this means we are focusing on UX. This might involve deploying applications, managing connections, interacting with Meshery features, and verifying the expected outcomes.</p>
<h3 id="implementation">
	Implementation
</h3>
<p>We will exclusively use the Bats Core framework and its built-in functionalities for writing E2E tests. This ensures consistency and leverages a well-established testing tool for shell scripts.</p>
<p><strong>Key Principles:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pure Bats Core:</strong> Avoid relying on external custom scripts or libraries beyond what Bats Core provides, while there might be occasional need to deviate from the library. Take in consideration that doing so all increases the possibility for bugs as well as our sustaining costs.</li>
<li><strong>Focus on <code>mesheryctl</code>:</strong> The tests should primarily interact with the <code>mesheryctl</code> CLI.</li>
<li><strong>Clear Assertions:</strong> Use Bats Core&rsquo;s assertion functions (<code>assert</code>, <code>assert_success</code>, <code>assert_failure</code>, <code>assert_output</code>, etc.) to verify expected outcomes.</li>
<li><strong>Setup and Teardown:</strong> Utilize <code>setup()</code> and <code>teardown()</code> functions to prepare the testing environment and clean up afterwards.</li>
<li><strong>Helper Scripts:</strong> If a custom script or function is absolutely necessary to facilitate testing (and cannot be achieved with standard Bats Core), it <strong>must</strong> be created as a <code>.bash</code> file within the <code>helpers</code> folder. Each helper script/function should have a clear description of its purpose within the file itself. Avoid inline custom scripting within the test files.</li>
<li><strong>Consistency</strong>:</li>
</ul>
<h4 id="test-naming-convention">
	Test Naming Convention
</h4>
<p>It must follow this naming convention</p>
<pre tabindex="0"><code>&lt;mesheryctl command&gt; [subcommand] &lt;execution context&gt; &lt;expected result&gt;
</code></pre><p><strong>Example:</strong></p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">@test <span class="s2">&#34;mesheryctl model view without model name should display an error&#34;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  ... <span class="nb">test</span> implementation ...
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="o">}</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="test-data">
	Test Data
</h4>
<p>If a command requries a specific id, name or any predefined value ensure that the data is created by your test or another test beforehand. Do not rely on external or uncontrolled data as it will lead to unexpected results.</p>
<p><strong>Example:</strong></p>
<p>In the following example, we must have create a model with the name <code>model-test</code> before creating or running the following test</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">@test <span class="s2">&#34;mesheryctl model view providing a model name should display model information&#34;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  run MESHERYCTL_BIN model view model-test
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  ... ...
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="o">}</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div><h4 id="writing-e2e-tests-with-bats-core">
	Writing E2E Tests with Bats Core
</h4>
<p>Official documentation is available at <a href="https://bats-core.readthedocs.io/en/stable/">https://bats-core.readthedocs.io/en/stable/</a></p>
<p>Github organization <a href="https://github.com/bats-core">https://github.com/bats-core</a> contains bats-core repository and also bats libraries repositoires</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p><strong>Basic Test Structure:</strong> A Bats test file consists of one or more test cases defined using the <code>@test</code> keyword.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="cp">#!/usr/bin/env bats
</span></span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">@test <span class="s2">&#34;Ensure mesheryctl version command works&#34;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  run mesheryctl version
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  assert_success
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  assert_output --partial <span class="s2">&#34;mesheryctl version&#34;</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="o">}</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div></li>
<li>
<p><strong>Interacting with <code>mesheryctl</code>:</strong> Execute <code>mesheryctl</code> commands within your test cases using the <code>run</code> command. Capture the output and exit status for assertions.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">@test <span class="s2">&#34;Deploy a sample application&#34;</span> <span class="o">{</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  run mesheryctl design apply -f samples/apps/nginx.yaml
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  assert_success
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  assert_output --partial <span class="s2">&#34;Successfully applied&#34;</span>
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl"><span class="o">}</span>
</span></span></code></pre></div></li>
<li>
<p><strong>Assertions:</strong> Use Bats Core&rsquo;s assertion functions to validate the results of your <code>mesheryctl</code> commands. Refer to the Bats Core documentation for a complete list of assertions.</p>
<ul>
<li><code>assert_success</code>: Checks if the command exited with a status code of 0.</li>
<li><code>assert_failure</code>: Checks if the command exited with a non-zero status code.</li>
<li><code>assert_output</code>: Checks if the command&rsquo;s output matches a given string.</li>
<li><code>assert_output --partial</code>: Checks if the command&rsquo;s output contains a given substring.</li>
<li><code>assert_equal</code>: Checks if two strings are equal.</li>
<li><code>assert_not_equal</code>: Checks if two strings are not equal.</li>
<li><code>assert_file_exists</code>: Checks if a file exists.</li>
<li><code>assert_file_contains</code>: Checks if a file contains a given string.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Setup and Teardown:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><code>setup()</code>: This function is executed before each test case within a file. Use it to set up the necessary environment for your tests (e.g., ensure Meshery is running, configure connections).</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>teardown()</code>: This function is executed after each test case within a file. Use it to clean up any resources created during the test (e.g., undeploy applications, reset configurations).</p>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Test Data:</strong> If your tests require specific input files (e.g., Kubernetes manifests), store them in a relevant directory (e.g., <code>tests/e2e/fixtures</code>).</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Error Handling:</strong> Consider how your tests will handle errors. Use appropriate assertions to check for expected failures and provide informative error messages.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="bug-reporting-during-test-implementation">
	Bug Reporting During Test Implementation
</h3>
<p>While implementing new E2E tests, you might discover bugs in <code>mesheryctl</code>. It is crucial to report these findings properly:</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p><strong>Create a New Issue:</strong> Navigate to the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/issues">meshery/meshery</a> repository on GitHub and click &ldquo;New issue.&rdquo;</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Use the <code>mesheryctl Bug Report</code> Template:</strong> Look for and select the &ldquo;mesheryctl Bug Report&rdquo; issue template. This template provides a structured format for reporting bugs related to the CLI.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Provide Detailed Information:</strong> Fill out the sections of the bug report template with as much detail as possible, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Steps to reproduce:</strong> Clearly outline the exact <code>mesheryctl</code> commands and environment setup that led to the bug.</li>
<li><strong>Expected behavior:</strong> Describe what you anticipated <code>mesheryctl</code> to do.</li>
<li><strong>Actual behavior:</strong> Describe what <code>mesheryctl</code> actually did. Include any error messages or unexpected output.</li>
<li><strong>Environment details:</strong> Provide information about your operating system, <code>mesheryctl</code> version (obtained using <code>mesheryctl version</code>), and the Meshery environment (e.g., local Docker, remote Kubernetes).</li>
<li><strong>Relevant logs:</strong> Include any relevant logs from <code>mesheryctl</code> or the Meshery server that might help diagnose the issue.</li>
<li><strong>Context:</strong> Explain the context in which you encountered the bug (e.g., while testing a specific feature).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Link to the Test:</strong> If the bug was discovered while writing a specific test, mention the test file and test case in the issue.</p>
</li>
</ol>

        </div>

<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js"
    integrity="sha256-FgpCb/KJQlLNfOu91ta32o/NMZxltwRo8QtmkMRdAu8=" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Contributing to Meshery CLI</h1>
          
          <p><code>mesheryctl</code> is written in Golang or the Go Programming Language. For development use <a href="https://go.dev/dl/">Go version 1.25+</a>. <code>mesheryctl</code> uses the <a href="https://github.com/spf13/cobra">Cobra</a> framework. A good first-step towards contributing to <code>mesheryctl</code> would be to familiarize yourself with the <a href="https://github.com/spf13/cobra#concepts">Cobra concepts</a>. For manipulating config files, <code>mesheryctl</code> uses <a href="https://github.com/spf13/viper">Viper</a>.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Meshery CLI Reference Documents</div>
<ul><li><a href="https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1q63sIGAuCnIeDs8PeM-0BAkNj8BBgPUXhLbe1Y-318o/edit#gid=0">Meshery Command Tracker</a>: Status of mesheryctl command implementation and platform compatibility.</li>
    <li><a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xRlFpElRmybJ3WacgPKXgCSiQ2poJl3iCCV1dAalf0k/edit#">Meshery CLI Commands and Documentation</a>: Detailed documentation of the `mesheryctl` commands.</li>
    <li><a href="https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/13Ir4gfaKoAX9r8qYjAFFl_U9ntke4X5ndREY1T7bnVs/edit?gid=1907616946#gid=1907616946">Meshery Test Plan</a>: Test cases for end-to-end testing of Meshery functionality.</li>
	<li><a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/labels/component%2Fmesheryctl">mesheryctl open issues and pull requests</a>: Matching the "component/mesheryctl" label.</li></ul></div>
<h3 id="designing-commands">
	Designing Commands
</h3>
<p>The <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli-guide/">Meshery CLI Style Guide</a> outlines the process by which new commands are designed and contains a collection of principles and conventions that need to be followed while designing <code>mesheryctl</code> commands. <code>mesheryctl</code> might be the interface that the users first have with Meshery. As such, <code>mesheryctl</code> needs to provide a great UX.</p>
<h3 id="building-cli">
	Building CLI
</h3>
<p>The <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/tree/master/mesheryctl"><code>/mesheryctl</code></a> folder contains the complete code for <code>mesheryctl</code>. Fork and clone the Meshery repo. <code>cd mesheryctl</code> to change directory mesheryctl&rsquo;s source. After making changes, run <code>make</code> in the <code>mesheryctl</code> folder to build the binary. You can then use the binary by, say, <code>./mesheryctl system start</code>.</p>
<h3 id="understand-model-and-configuration-data">
	Understand Model and Configuration Data
</h3>
<p>A central <code>struct</code> is maintained in the <code>mesheryctl/internal/cli/root/config/config.go</code> file. These are updated and should be used for getting the Meshery configuration.</p>
<p>Updates to this central <code>struct</code> is made through updates in <code>Context</code> with setter functions. The changes made in this central <code>struct</code> are reflected back in the Meshery configuration file (<code>.meshery/config.yaml</code>).</p>
<h3 id="logging">
	Logging
</h3>
<p>For logs, <code>mesheryctl</code> uses <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshkit">MeshKit</a>.</p>
<h3 id="documenting">
	Documenting
</h3>
<p>The documentation pages for <code>mesheryctl</code> reference are made with the help of the Cobra Golang framework and use of GitHub Actions. The <a href="/v0.9/reference/mesheryctl/">Meshery CLI Reference</a> is autogenerated based on docs sections in each of <code>mesheryctl</code>&rsquo;s Golang files. Meshery CLI Reference pages are updated each time a change to its respective <code>mesheryctl</code> Golang file is merged into the project&rsquo;s <code>master</code> branch. This approach to documentation facilitates a single source of truth for CLI syntax and command behavior, which results in higher quality reference and a reduction in the toil involved in keeping documentation up-to-date. To contribute to the Meshery CLI Reference, follow these steps:</p>
<ul>
<li>Go to the required command file in which the documentation has to be created/updated (mainly under /mesheryctl/internal/cli/root/&hellip;)</li>
<li>Then, edit the Cobra macro variables present in the each file. An example is given below for reference.</li>
</ul>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">var startCmd = &amp;cobra.Command{
Use:   &#34;start&#34;,
Short: &#34;Start Meshery&#34;,
Long:  &#39;Start Meshery and each of its components.&#39;,
Args:  cobra.NoArgs,
Example:
// Start meshery
mesheryctl system start

// To create a new context for in-cluster Kubernetes deployments and set the new context as your current-context
mesheryctl system context create k8s -p kubernetes -s,
Annotations: linkScreenshot,
...</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<p>The variables present in above sample will be used in creating the doc pages for the specific command</p>
<p>Also, if the screenshot is present in the command, an <code>Annotation</code> macro variable (of <code>map[string]string</code> type) containing the <code>link</code> and the <code>caption</code> has to be added at the bottom of the <code>Examples</code> field in the command file. The image file has to be included in the <code>docs/content/en/reference/images</code> folder in <strong>PNG</strong> format. The screenshot field is given for reference below</p>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">var linkDocPatternApply = map[string]string{
	&#34;link&#34;:    &#34;![pattern-apply-usage](/reference/images/patternApply.png)&#34;,
	&#34;caption&#34;: &#34;Usage of mesheryctl design apply&#34;,
}
...
Example:
// apply a pattern file
mesheryctl design apply -f [file | URL]

// deploy a saved design
mesheryctl design apply [design-name]
Annotations: linkDocPatternApply,
...</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Avoid documentation being overwritten</div>
<p>It is advised not to modify the changes in <code>docs</code> folder, rather should be done in <code>mesheryctl</code> folder as the changes will get overwritten by the CI workflows.</div></p>
<h3 id="adding-newremoving-existing-commands-in-the-reference-index">
	Adding New/Removing Existing commands in the reference index
</h3>
<p>Though the command page is generated automatically by the Cobra CLI library, there are chances where the command does not appear in the <a href="/v0.9/reference/mesheryctl/">reference index page</a>. In such cases, the command details must be manually added to the reference index YAML file. This is generally done by editing the below two files:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/blob/master/docs/data/mesheryctlcommands/cmds.yml">cmds.yml</a> - The YAML file containing the data about the commands</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/blob/master/docs/content/en/reference/mesheryctl/_index.md">_index.md</a> - The markdown page of the command reference documentation</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="preserving-manually-added-documentation">
	Preserving Manually Added Documentation
</h3>
<p><code>mesheryctl</code> uses Cobra CLI library and GitHub Actions to automate the generation of command documentation pages. On occasion, additional documentation beyond that included in the <code>mesheryctl</code> Golang files is ideal to capture and include in the CLI reference pages. Contributors are encouraged to add more usage examples, screenshots to any of the CLI reference pages. To protect any manually added content and ensure it remains intact after regeneration, create a separate Hugo <code>shortcode</code> file. Follow file naming scheme outlined below:</p>
<p>If your mesheryctl docs end like this, add a shortcode at the end of the file. An example is given below</p>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">Example:
// apply a pattern file
mesheryctl design apply -f [file | URL]

// deploy a saved design
mesheryctl design apply [design-name],
Annotations: linkDocPatternApply,
...
&lt;pre class=&#39;codeblock-pre&#39;&gt;
&lt;div class=&#39;codeblock&#39;&gt;
      --config string   path to config file (default &#34;/home/runner/.meshery/config.yaml&#34;)
  -t, --token string    Path to token file default from current context
  -v, --verbose         verbose output

&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;/pre&gt;
{{&lt; permalink-of-file &gt;}}</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<h2 id="quality">
	Quality
</h2>
<h3 id="linting">
	Linting
</h3>
<p><code>mesheryctl</code> uses <a href="https://github.com/golangci/golangci-lint">golangci-lint</a>. See the .github/workflow/ci.yaml for syntax used during Meshery&rsquo;s build process.</p>
<h3 id="testing">
	Testing
</h3>
<h3 id="key-test-writing-principles">
	Key Test Writing Principles
</h3>
<p>The following key principles should be taken to mind when writing tests:</p>
<ol>
<li>Golang’s standard library will be used to write tests.</li>
<li>The tests should cover all possible use cases and not just the happy paths.</li>
<li>Integration tests should contain the keyword <strong>“Integration”</strong> in the title and should be marked to be skipped under unit testing. (See below)</li>
<li><strong>Fixtures</strong> are mock/raw data to use(for e.g. API response to mock an HTTP call).</li>
<li><strong>Testdata</strong> is the expected response of mesheryctl commands or functions.</li>
<li>The mock data and the expected responses are stored in the <strong>golden files</strong>.</li>
<li>Table formatted tests are performed on functions and commands.</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/blob/master/mesheryctl/pkg/utils/fixtures/validate.version.github.golden">mesheryctl/pkg/utils/fixtures/validate.version.github.golden</a> file needs to be updated regularly.</li>
<li>The version in utils.NewTestHelper() should be updated regularly.</li>
<li>Golden files should be updated synchronously as API responses, mesheryctl outputs are updated.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>References</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://github.com/jarcoal/httpmock">jarcoal/httpmock</a></li>
<li><a href="https://medium.com/swlh/unit-testing-cli-programs-in-go-6275c85af2e7">Unit testing CLIs in Go</a></li>
<li><a href="https://gianarb.it/blog/golang-mockmania-cli-command-with-cobra">How to test CLI commands with Go and Cobra</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NAvt6B5kNIQ">Contributing to Meshery API Swagger Documentation</a></li>
</ul>
<h4 id="unit-tests">
	Unit Tests
</h4>
<p>Unit tests and integration tests are essential to make each mesheryctl release robust and of high quality. Below you will find guidelines to write unit tests and integration tests and examples of how they are implemented in mesheryctl.</p>
<p>Unit test code coverage reports can be found in the <a href="https://app.codecov.io/gh/meshery/meshery/">CodeCov logs</a>. <em>Note: GitHub login may be required for access.</em></p>
<p>This format should reference an external file where your manual changes are stored. These files should be present at the folder path (<code>_includes/mesheryctl/</code>). Any content added using this method will not be altered during the documentation generation process, but instead will be included post-auto doc generation. When making new changes or additions, understand that these additional details are positioned at the end their given CLI reference page, so bear this in mind as you organize and present your additional command details.</p>
<h3 id="integration-tests">
	Integration Tests
</h3>
<p><strong>Marking integration tests under unit tests</strong></p>
<p>Since there is no straightforward way to mark unit tests and integration tests differently. Here we use the <code>--short</code> flag while running tests to differentiate between unit tests and integration tests.</p>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">func TestPreflightCmdIntegration(t *testing.T) {
   // skipping this integration test with --short flag
   if testing.Short() {
       t.Skip(&#34;skipping integration test&#34;)
   }
}</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<p>In the above code sample, the test is marked with <strong>“Integration”</strong> in the title and if a <code>--short</code> flag is passed with the command, this test is skipped.</p>
<h3 id="running-tests-in-github-workflows">
	Running tests in GitHub workflows
</h3>
<h4 id="unit-tests-1">
	Unit tests
</h4>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">go test --short ./... -race -coverprofile=coverage.txt -covermode=atomic</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<h4 id="integration-tests-1">
	Integration tests
</h4>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">go test -run Integration ./... -race -coverprofile=coverage.txt -covermode=atomic</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<p>To update golden files with the test output use the <code>--update</code> flag:</p>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">var update = flag.Bool(&#34;update&#34;, false, &#34;update golden files&#34;)</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<h4 id="end-to-end-tests">
	End-to-end Tests
</h4>
<p>End-to-end testing of mesheryctl uses the Bash Automated Testing System (BATS) framework to define and execute CLI tests. See <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli-tests/">Contributing to Meshery CLI End-to-End Tests</a></p>

        </div>

<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js"
    integrity="sha256-FgpCb/KJQlLNfOu91ta32o/NMZxltwRo8QtmkMRdAu8=" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
            <h1>Contributing to Model Components</h1>
          
          <p><strong>Components are defined by schemas.</strong> Each component&rsquo;s structure, capabilities, and metadata follow the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/tree/master/schemas/constructs/v1beta1/component">Component schema</a> in <code>meshery/schemas</code>. When creating or modifying components, ensure they conform to the schema specification. See <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-schemas/">Contributing to Schemas</a> for details.</p>
<p>In Meshery, a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">Components</a> is a fundamental building block used to represent and define the infrastructure under management. Each component provides granular and specific support for your infrastructure and applications. Once registered with Meshery Server (in the <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/">Registry</a>), components are available for inclusion in <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">Designs</a> that you create. Components can be created and published by anyone, allowing you to share you custom extensions with the community.</p>
<h2 id="overview-of-steps-to-create-components">
	Overview of Steps to Create Components
</h2>
<p><strong>Prework:</strong></p>
<!-- 1. [Component Identification](#component-identification) -->
<ol>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-components/#component-classification">Component Classification</a></li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Development:</strong></p>
<ol>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-components/#component-definitions">Component Definition</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-components/#component-customization">Component Customization</a></li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Postwork:</strong></p>
<ol>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-components/#component-testing">Component Testing</a></li>

</ol>
<h2 id="prework">
	Prework
</h2>
<p><a id="component-classification"></a></p>
<h3 id="1-understand-model-generation-and-packaging">
	1. Understand Model Generation and Packaging
</h3>
<div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Prerequisite Reading</div>
<p>Components are defined and packaged in context of a Model. Be sure to first read and understand <a href='/project/contributing/contributing-models'>how models are created and packaged</a> before attempting to create a new component. Without a model defined first, they component will be homeless.</div></p>
<p><a id="component-customization"></a></p>
<h3 id="2-customize-component-form-based-representation">
	2. Customize Component Form-based Representation
</h3>
<p>Each component has any number of customizable properties in the form of metadata. The metadata provides additional details about the component, enhancing its capabilities. Metadata can be attached to components to customize their behavior. The metadata can be used to define the component&rsquo;s behavior, appearance, and interactions with other components.</p>
<h4 id="customize-component-form-based-representation">
	Customize Component Form-based Representation
</h4>
<p>Components optionally have a UI schema, which is a JSON object that describes how a form should be rendered. It can be passed to JSON forms and is categorized into controls or layouts. The UI schema object follows the form field hierarchy&rsquo;s tree structure and defines how each property should be rendered. For example, it can specify the order of controls, their visibility, and the layout.</p>
<p>Some UI schema elements have an options property that allows for further configuration of the rendering result. These configuration options are often renderer specific and need to be looked up. Some commonly used options include:</p>
<p><code>ui:order</code>: An array of field names in the order in which they should appear
<code>ui:widget</code>: The name of an alternative widget to use for the field
<code>ui:field</code>: The name of a custom field
<code>classNames</code>: The class names to put on the component</p>
<p>Meshery UI uses the <code>react-jsonschema-form</code> library to render forms. See the <a href="https://rjsf-team.github.io/react-jsonschema-form/docs/">RJSF documentation</a> for more information.</p>
<h4 id="customize-component-visual-representation">
	Customize Component Visual Representation
</h4>
<p>Meshery contributors who want to customize the visual representation of a Meshery component can do so by modifying the component&rsquo;s metadata. This metadata includes fields for specifying the component&rsquo;s:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>SVG</strong>: The SVG file used to represent the component visually.</li>
<li><strong>Primary Color</strong>: The primary color used for the component in hex format.</li>
<li><strong>Secondary Color</strong>: The secondary color used for the component in hex format.</li>
<li><strong>Shape</strong>: The basic shape of the component, such as a circle or square.</li>
<li><strong>isAnnotation</strong>: A boolean value that indicates whether the component is an annotation or is <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">semantically meaningful</a>.</li>
</ul>
<details>

</details>
<p>Contributors can also override these settings for individual components if needed. For example, if a component has a different SVG color than its model, you can specify a custom SVG color for that component.</p>
<p>Component icons will be written to the <code>/meshmodel/components/&lt;model-name&gt;/icon/...</code> directory upon registration.</p>
<h2 id="development">
	Development
</h2>
<p><a id="component-definitions"></a></p>
<h3 id="3-create-a-component-definition-as-a-json-file">
	3. Create a Component Definition as a JSON file
</h3>
<p>Create a relationship definition as a JSON file, placing this new definition file into its respective model folder (see <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-models/">Contributing to Models</a>). Relationship definition files are commonly named  <code>relationships.yaml</code> as a convention, however, this name is not required. A model may include any number of relationship definitions. Include the following attributes in your relationship definition:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>kind</code>: The genre of component (e.g., <code>Pod</code>).</li>
<li><code>model</code>: The model to which the component belongs (e.g., <code>kubernetes</code>).</li>
<li><code>version</code>: The version of the component definition (e.g., <code>v1.0.0</code>).</li>
<li><code>description</code>: A characterization of the component, its purpose and behavior.</li>
</ul>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Use Existing Components as Examples</div>
<p>Browse the <a href='https://github.com/meshery/meshery/tree/master/server/meshmodel'>existing components in the Meshery repository</a> to find examples of how to existing component, using them as a template.</div></p>
<h2 id="postwork">
	Postwork
</h2>
<p><a id="component-testing"></a></p>
<h4 id="4-component-authoring-best-practices-and-considerations">
	4. Component Authoring Best Practices and Considerations
</h4>
<h5 id="general">
	General
</h5>
<ol>
<li>Use camelCasing as the formatting convention.</li>
<li>Increment the component definition using the <code>version</code> property with each change published.</li>
</ol>
<p><a class="anchorjs-link" id="component-contribution"></a></p>
<h4 id="5-contribute-your-component-to-the-meshery-project">
	5. Contribute your component to the Meshery project
</h4>
<p>Submit a pull request to the Meshery repository with your new component definition, so that all users can benefit from the component(s) you have defined.</p>
<p>Keeping your component definition in a separate file allows for easier management and review of the component(s) you have defined.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Keeping your custom Components private</div>
<p>Alternatively, if you would like to keep the component definition private, you can bundle your component(s) in a custom model, import the custom model into your Meshery deployment. Your private component definition(s) will be registered in your Meshery Server&rsquo;s <a href='/concepts/logical/registry'>registry</a> and available for use within your Meshery deployment.</div></p>

        </div>

<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js"
    integrity="sha256-FgpCb/KJQlLNfOu91ta32o/NMZxltwRo8QtmkMRdAu8=" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

            <h1>Contributing to Meshery Docker Extension</h1>
          
          <h2 id="prerequisites">
	Prerequisites
</h2>
<p>To start contributing to Meshery Docker Extension, make sure you have <a href="https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/">Docker</a> installed on your system.</p>
<h3 id="docker-extension-for-meshery">
	Docker Extension for Meshery
</h3>
<p>The Docker Extension for Meshery extends Docker Desktop’s position as the cloud native developer’s go-to Kubernetes environment with easy access to the next layer of cloud native infrastructure. The extension provides a seamless experience for developers to manage and monitor their Kubernetes applications and services.</p>
<h4 id="using-docker-desktop">
	Using Docker Desktop
</h4>
<ol>
<li>
<p>Navigate to the Extensions Marketplace of Docker Desktop.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>From the Dashboard, select Add Extensions in the menu bar or open the Extensions Marketplace from the menu options.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<a href="/project/contributing/images/docker-extension-browse.png">
  <img style="width:350px;" src="/project/contributing/images/docker-extension-browse.png">
</a>
<ol start="3">
<li>Navigate to Meshery in the Marketplace and press install.</li>
</ol>
<a href="/project/contributing/images/docker-extension.png">
  <img style="width:90%" src="/project/contributing/images/docker-extension.png">
</a>
<p>OR</p>
<p>You can visit the <a href="https://hub.docker.com/extensions/meshery/docker-extension-meshery">Docker Hub</a> marketplace to directly install Meshery extension in your Docker Desktop.</p>
<h4 id="using-docker-cli">
	Using <code>Docker CLI</code>
</h4>
<p>Meshery runs as a set of containers inside your Docker Desktop virtual machine.</p>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">docker extension install meshery/docker-extension-meshery</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<h2 id="set-up-the-server">
	Set up the server
</h2>
<p>In the root directory of meshery, run the following command:</p>
<h3 id="to-installupdate-the-ui-dependencies">
	To install/update the UI dependencies:
</h3>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">make ui-setup</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<h3 id="start-the-server-locally">
	Start the server locally
</h3>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">make server</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<p>This will ensure that the server is up and running at port 9081</p>
<h2 id="set-up-docker-extension-locally">
	Set up docker extension Locally
</h2>
<p>Open another terminal while the server is running,
Go inside the docker-extension directory 

<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">cd install/docker-extension</code>
	</div>
</pre>
</p>
<h3 id="build-and-export-ui">
	Build and export UI
</h3>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">make ui-build</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<h3 id="ui-development-server">
	UI Development Server
</h3>
<p>If you want to work on the Docker UI, it will be a good idea to use the included UI development server. You can run the UI development server by running the following command:


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">make ui</code>
	</div>
</pre>
</p>
<p>Now the meshery docker-extension is up and running.</p>
<h3 id="linking-the-docker-extension-locally">
	Linking the docker extension locally
</h3>
<p>To see the changes reflected in the docker extension locally and open the devTools window, we can run the command:


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">make link</code>
	</div>
</pre>
</p>
<p>Now that our local development environment is connected with the meshery docker extension, we can start contributing to it.</p>

        </div>

<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js"
    integrity="sha256-FgpCb/KJQlLNfOu91ta32o/NMZxltwRo8QtmkMRdAu8=" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

<script>
    $(document).ready(function () {

        var toc = $('#TOC');

        
        
        
        
        var hasH1 = $('.td-content h1').length > 0;
        var topSelector = hasH1 ? 'h1' : 'h2';
        var subSelector = hasH1 ? 'h2, h3' : 'h3';

        sections = $('.td-content ' + topSelector);

        $.each(sections, function (idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if (!section.hasClass('noTOC')) {
                var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
                var parent = $("#" + div_id)
                var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text + '">' + div_text + '</a></li>';
                $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil(topSelector);
            $.each(contenders, function (idx, contender) {
                if (!$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && $(contender).is(subSelector)) {
                    var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                    var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                    var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text + '">' + contender_text + '</a></li>';
                    children.append(content);
                }
            })
            $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function (e) {
            
            let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
            
            $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {
                if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
                    
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
                if ($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
                    $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
                    $(this).addClass('selected');
                }
            });
        })
    });
</script>

            <h1>Meshery Documentation Structure and Organization</h1>
          
          <p>Providing well-structured, easy-to-navigate documentation tailored for a diverse audience—from beginners to experts.</p>
<h2 id="target-audience">
	Target Audience
</h2>
<p>We first identify <strong>who</strong> this documentation serves before diving into how it’s organized. By clarifying different user personas, we can better direct them to relevant sections:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Users</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>New Users</strong>: Individuals just getting started with Meshery, needing a straightforward, guided setup.</li>
<li><strong>Advanced Users</strong>: Those who already have some experience and want deeper insights or specialized use cases.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Contributors &amp; System Integrators</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Open Source Contributors</strong>: Developers who extend Meshery’s features, fix bugs, or contribute documentation.</li>
<li><strong>System Integrators</strong>: Professionals adding Meshery into existing ecosystems or building custom integrations.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Administrators</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Operators, DevOps, SREs, IT professionals, system administrators, security specialists</strong>: Responsible for large-scale deployments, performance tuning, security, and overall upkeep of Meshery in production environments.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="high-level-outline">
	High-Level Outline
</h2>
<p>After defining our audience, we introduce the <strong>overall structure</strong> of Meshery’s documentation. Each section below addresses a different need, level of expertise, or user focus.</p>
<ol>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#overview-and-installation-user-persona">Overview and Installation (User Persona)</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#tasks--operations-user-guide">Tasks &amp; Operations (User Guide)</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#administrators-guide-advanced-topics">Administrator’s Guide (Advanced Topics)</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#integrations-and-extensions-all-personas">Integrations and Extensions (All Personas)</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#tutorials-all-personas">Tutorials (All Personas)</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#reference--resources-all-personas">Reference &amp; Resources (All Personas)</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-docs-structure/#contributing-and-community-all-personas">Contributing and Community (All Personas)</a></li>
</ol>
<h2 id="overview-and-installation-user-persona">
	Overview and Installation (User Persona)
</h2>
<p>This section focuses on giving new and experienced users an overarching understanding of Meshery, including basic setup, installation options, and general operations.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Getting Started:</strong> Overview of Meshery, installation options, prerequisites, and setup instructions.</li>
<li><strong>Installation Guides:</strong> Step-by-step instructions for installing Meshery on different platforms (local, cloud, minikube).
<ul>
<li><strong>Configuration Guides:</strong> How to configure Meshery in these environments.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Tasks &amp; Operations</strong> (User Guide)</li>
<li><strong>Concepts:</strong> Basic Meshery concepts (clusters, pods, deployments, services), terminology glossary.</li>
<li><strong>Use Cases:</strong> Demonstrations of common scenarios (web app deployment, data processing pipeline).</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="getting-started-new-users">
	Getting Started (New Users)
</h3>
<p>This section provides a concise, hands-on introduction for newcomers, referring back to “Overview and Installation” for more details.</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Introduction to Meshery</strong>:
<ul>
<li>What is Meshery? Why use it? Key features, benefits, use cases.</li>
<li>Basic terminology glossary.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Installation and Setup</strong>
<ul>
<li>Prerequisites, system requirements.</li>
<li>Platform-specific installation guides (local, cloud, air-gapped).</li>
<li>Configuration guides, Verifying Installation.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>First Steps</strong>
<ul>
<li>Basic Meshery UI/CLI walkthrough.</li>
<li>Deploying a simple application.</li>
<li>Connecting to a cluster.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="concepts-all-personas">
	Concepts (All Personas)
</h3>
<p>Concept pages describe <strong>what</strong> a particular aspect of Meshery is, but not <strong>how</strong> to do it step-by-step. They provide background knowledge and link out to related tasks or tutorials.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Architectural Concepts:</strong> Meshery architecture, design, and implementation details. Diagrams illustrating interaction between components, resource dependencies.</li>
<li><strong>Logical Concepts:</strong> Meshery components, resources, and relationships. Diagrams illustrating interaction between components, resource dependencies.</li>
</ul>
<!-- - **Deep Dives:** Detailed explanations of core Meshery components. -->
<h3 id="tasks--operations-user-guide">
	Tasks &amp; Operations (User Guide)
</h3>
<p>A task page shows how to do a <strong>single</strong> thing, typically by giving a short sequence of steps. Task pages have minimal explanation, but often provide links to conceptual topics that provide related background and knowledge.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Task Guides:</strong> Step-by-step instructions for common tasks (deploying applications, managing resources).</li>
<li><strong>Configuration Management:</strong> Designing infrastructure, managing configuration files.</li>
<li><strong>Lifecycle Management:</strong> Discoverying, registering, configuring infrastructure
<ul>
<li>Discovery (MeshSync): Greenfield/Brownfield scenarios.</li>
<li>Managing Connections: Registering, updating, and deleting connections.</li>
<li>Managing Credentials: Registering, updating, and deleting credentials.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Performance Management:</strong> Load testing, performance monitoring, resource usage analysis.</li>
</ul>
<!-- - **Workflows:** Step-by-step procedures for common tasks (rolling updates, blue-green deployments). -->
<h3 id="administrators-guide-platform-engineer--operator-persona-advanced-topics">
	Administrator&rsquo;s Guide (Platform Engineer &amp; Operator Persona, Advanced Topics)
</h3>
<p>Designed for platform engineers, operators, DevOps, and other advanced users who require deeper insights into Meshery’s configuration, security, and maintenance.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Performance Optimization:</strong> Resource usage analysis, profiling tools, tuning techniques.</li>
<li><strong>GitOps / DevOps &amp; CI/CD</strong>: Integrating Meshery with continuous integration and deployment pipelines.</li>
<li><strong>Best Practices:</strong> Recommendations for securing the Meshery, monitoring performance, managing versions.</li>
<li><strong>Advanced Concepts:</strong> Advanced Meshery concepts, features, and capabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Air-gapped Environments:</strong> Deploying Meshery in air-gapped environments.</li>
<li><strong>Troubleshooting Guides:</strong> Common errors, debugging, tips.</li>
<li><strong>Multi-Meshery Management:</strong> Federation, cluster federation, GitOps for configuration management.</li>
<li><strong>Security and Compliance:</strong> Security best practices, compliance requirements, vulnerability management.</li>
<li><strong>Backup and Recovery:</strong> Backup strategies, disaster recovery planning, data restoration.</li>
<li><strong>Scaling and High Availability:</strong> Scaling Meshery, high availability, load balancing, failover strategies.</li>
<li><strong>Monitoring and Logging:</strong> Monitoring Meshery, logging, alerting, observability tools.</li>
<li><strong>Upgrading Meshery:</strong> Version compatibility, upgrade paths, release notes, rollback procedures.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="integrations-and-extensions-all-personas">
	Integrations and Extensions (All Personas)
</h3>
<p>Meshery’s extensibility allows for seamless integration with existing systems and the addition of new capabilities through adapters, plugins, and extensions.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Extensibility:</strong> Customizing Meshery with plugins, adapters, and extensions.
<ul>
<li><strong>APIs:</strong> Simple summary of Meshery&rsquo;s APIs.</li>
<li><strong>Extension Points:</strong> Providers, plugins, adapters, modules.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Integrations:</strong> Meshery Models. Integrating Meshery with different infrastructure and systems.</li>
<li><strong>Extensions:</strong> List of all of Meshery adapters, plugins, and modules for different extension points.
<ul>
<li><strong>Adapters:</strong> Integrating Meshery with different infrastructure and extended capabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Plugins:</strong> Extended capabilities for Meshery.</li>
<li><strong>Remote Providers:</strong> Remote providers for additional functionality.</li>
<li><strong>Security and Identity:</strong> Authentication, authorization, secrets management, vulnerability scanning.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="tutorials-all-personas">
	Tutorials (All Personas)
</h3>
<p>A tutorial page shows how to accomplish a goal that is larger than a single task. Typically a tutorial page has several sections, each of which has a sequence of steps. For example, a tutorial might provide a walkthrough of a code sample that illustrates a certain feature of Kubernetes. Tutorials can include surface-level explanations, but should link to related concept topics for deep explanations.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Tutorials:</strong> Dedicated walk-throughs with labs and step-by-step instructions using Meshery&rsquo;s features.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="reference--resources-all-personas">
	Reference &amp; Resources (All Personas)
</h3>
<p>A component tool reference page shows the description and flag options output for a Meshery component. For example, a component tool reference page might describe the Meshery CLI and explain the role it plays as an application once it is deployed, scaled, and updated. Typically, component tool reference pages don&rsquo;t include sequences of steps, but instead provide links to tasks or tutorials.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Command References:</strong> Detailed explanations and examples for <code>mesheryctl</code> commands, API resources.</li>
<li><strong>API Documentation:</strong> Comprehensive reference for Meshery API objects and fields.</li>
<li><strong>Custom Resource Definition Reference:</strong> Comprehensive reference for Meshery CRDs.</li>
<li><strong>Release Notes:</strong> Detailed information about version changes, new features, deprecations.</li>
<li><strong>Glossary:</strong> Definitions of common terms, acronyms, and abbreviations.</li>
<li><strong>Vulnerability Reports:</strong> Security advisories, CVEs, and vulnerability reports.</li>
</ul>
<h3 id="contributing-and-community-all-personas">
	Contributing and Community (All Personas)
</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>External Resources:</strong> Links to blogs, community forums, case studies, books, training materials.</li>
<li><strong>Contributing Guide:</strong> How to contribute documentation, code, and other resources to the project.</li>
<li><strong>Community:</strong> Highlight community forums, events, contributor guidelines, recognition.</li>
<li><strong>FAQ:</strong> Answers to frequently asked questions.</li>
</ul>
<p>This high-level outline provides a comprehensive framework for structuring the Meshery documentation, catering to diverse user needs while ensuring information is readily accessible and actionable. By further refining each section with specific content recommendations and considering the needs of specific personas, the documentation can effectively serve as a valuable resource for everyone interacting with Meshery.</p>

        </div>
